doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: How Budd came to attend Dick Gibson's jazz parties
summary: From Cliff Leeman and Peanuts Hucko to the 1969 invitation, and meeting Gibson's wife again.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: Wow. You get around the circuit of the jazz parties?

Yes, I did. The first one was at the Gibson one, which started — I never heard of these things but I read about them in the jazz magazines. One time at Eddie Condon’s place, Cliff Lehman, who was a drummer in those days with the bunch around Condon’s, and he said “you like music so much, there’s a jazz party in Colorado that you’d certainly like to go.” And I said “yeah I’ve heard of it.” He said “well maybe you could get to go if you write to them and ask for in invitation.” But you couldn’t get one in 1968, it was sold out every time. The next year, Peanuts Huckoe was working in Cleveland in a restaurant there in a band, and I had known him around Condon’s place, and he was on his way, moving from New York to the coast where he lives out in the west. And he was playing a week or two in this restaurant and he said “I have a Sunday engagement in Pittsburgh and I’m going to fly down there,” but he said “I’m driving out to California and I have a truck, a U-Haul truck,” and he says “I don’t want to leave that downtown, it might get broken into. Could I leave that truck at your house?” And I said yeah, sure could. So my son, he was led to drive that truck out and he left it over the weekend. And Peanuts went to Pittsburgh and came back the next day and he stayed overnight with me and my wife. And he was going west and he was going to stop and play at the Gibson party that year. And he said “maybe I could get you seats at that.” So I telephoned Mr. Gibson and Gibson said no, they’re sold out, he couldn’t do it. But he said well see — ask next year perhaps. And the next year my wife and I were going somewhere, we were in New York, and The World’s Greatest Jazz Band, which Gibson promoted, was playing at a hotel and we went down to see it. And Gibson of course was from Alabama and so was my wife. And we met and he talked to her, and Ralph Sutton was playing in the band at that time and I had known him from the Condon days, and Ralph said “I’ll see what I can do to get Gibson to get you to the party,” and it turned out we were invited to go, and my wife said that’s ‘cause Mr. Gibson and I, she’s from Alabama and I think Mr. Gibson knew I was from Alabama and that’s how you got invited. So we were invited to go to the party and that was in 1969, and we couldn’t wait to go. And that’s the year I was elected to the Board of Trustees of the AMA. And their first meeting was on that very weekend and I had to call Gibson and say I can’t possibly come, but I hope I can come next year. And he let us come, and I went the next year, 1970, and I went every year, almost, until it quit. And I think Marjorie knows — was it the final one we went to Marjorie? was. And we became great friends. I saw Mattie Gibson here and she was just so delighted, and made a big fuss over me. I’ve done the same thing about her because she was important to me. And she even said now this is something different but — you might want to erase it — she said “I’ll go and speak to Dick and Thomasai, he’ll be so glad because they are not on the best of terms I’m afraid. And I said “how is he?” “He’s doing pretty well” and so forth. And his son Josh is with him and so forth. But she was very nice. She’s a super lady I think to be thinking about that. Like so many of those people they’ve been exceptionally nice and they are good to me.
Well music seems to bring people together like that, don’t you think?
Well this has been a fascinating talk, and you know I think next time we run into each other at one of these parties we should do this again.
